title: Recollecting the teaching
hook: one teacher makes a hard thing click; another makes an easy thing impossible. what does 'well taught' mean?
tomorrow: who practices well, and why call them to mind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, buddhanussati: thus indeed is he, the Buddha's qualities called to mind until conscience is as clear as standing face to face. Next, the teaching.

A good teacher can make a hard thing click in one afternoon. A muddled one can make an easy thing impossible. Same subject, different teaching. Yesterday's question asked what makes a teaching well taught, and the old chant opens on exactly that word: svakkhato bhagavata dhammo. Well taught by the Blessed One is the dhamma. Buddhaghosa stops on that first word and asks what it means.
screen: `A HARD THING CLICKS.` → `SAME SUBJECT, DIFFERENT TEACHING.` → `SVAKKHATO: WELL TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: His answer borrows a phrase the suttas use again and again: good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, right in meaning and in wording. And he applies it at every size. A single verse, good in its first line, its middle and its last. A whole sutta, from its setting to its close. The whole path: good conduct at the beginning, calm and insight in the middle, freedom at the end. Well taught means it holds together at every scale, with no filler. Now a neighbor. In the Torah, Moses tells Israel the commandment isn't hidden or far off, and isn't up in heaven where someone must go and fetch it. In the King James words: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Here's what they share: a teaching meant to be close, spoken and lived, not admired from a distance. And one honest difference. Deuteronomy's word is a commandment from God, part of a covenant with a people. The dhamma is described as something the Buddha found and taught, with no one commanding it, to be seen by each person for themselves. Different roots, the same nearness. A teaching that's well taught doesn't stay on the page.
screen: `GOOD IN THE BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.` · `A VERSE, A SUTTA, THE WHOLE PATH.` · `DEUTERONOMY: VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.` · `A COMMANDMENT, OR A TEACHING FOUND.` · then, large: `WELL TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write svakkhato, well taught, slowly. Under it, write one thing someone once taught you well: a coach, a grandparent, a friend. Look at the two lines together and notice what made the second one stick.
Recollecting the teaching: calling the dhamma's qualities to mind, starting with svakkhato, well taught.
Keep this one: well taught, good in the beginning, the middle and the end. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the recollection of the dhamma, svakkhato bhagavata dhammo, in daily and temple chanting; as a meditation its qualities are called to mind one at a time, as Visuddhimagga 7 describes.

fork.setup: your cousin's coach writes one sentence on the whiteboard each week, and the team actually uses it. by today's lesson, what makes it well taught?
options: it's short, so it's easy for everyone to memorize.
it holds together, and it's close enough to use in a game.
it comes from someone with the right title and rank.
fork.reveal: well taught means good from beginning to end, and near enough to live: in thy mouth and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.

original.note: Pali: well taught, well proclaimed. The first quality in the recollection of the dhamma.

chat.says: Ava asked if the dhamma is something you believe or something you do. what do i say
options: Something you do and check: well taught start to finish, and near enough to live.
Something you believe. You accept the Buddha's words first; practice comes after.
Neither. It's basically the same as every religion's rules, just older.
chat.meaning: Buddhaghosa reads well taught as good in the beginning, middle and end: a path of conduct, calm and insight, meant to be lived and seen for yourself.

tie.story: Svakkhato: good in the beginning, middle and end, near enough to live.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 7 (recollection of the dhamma: 'well proclaimed' because good in the beginning, the middle and the end, applied to a stanza, a sutta and the whole dispensation, virtue as the beginning, serenity and insight the middle, fruition and nibbana the end)

Recollection of the dhamma (svakkhato bhagavata dhammo …), as in SN 11.3; the stock phrase 'good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing', as in DN 2

notes: Wisdom shape with the unity thread: shared idea (a teaching meant to be near, spoken and lived) in each tradition's own source (Visuddhimagga 7 and the suttas' stock phrase, paraphrased; Deuteronomy 30:14 quoted from the KJV), plus one honest difference (a commandment from God within a covenant vs a teaching described as found and taught by the Buddha, seen by each for themselves). No ranking. A Keeper of each tradition should confirm the difference is described fairly.
Deuteronomy 30:14 is quoted in the KJV; the JPS 1917 wording is believed identical. Confirm, since the lesson frames it as the Torah's own words.

Visuddhimagga 7 paraphrased: svakkhato as good in the beginning, middle and end, applied to a stanza, a sutta and the dispensation (virtue; serenity and insight; fruition and nibbana). Confirm the stanza breakdown as told ('its first line, its middle and its last').
The dhamma recollection was taught on day 1444 through ehipassiko (come and see); this day takes svakkhato through Buddhaghosa's reading to avoid repeating it.
